problems.title: The \(0.75\) lower constant in Lemma 4.5 fails inside the stated initialization set
problems.source_location: Lemma 4.5, PDF p. 7; proof in Appendix E.4, PDF p. 25.
claim: Lemma 4.5, PDF p. 7 and Appendix E.4, PDF p. 25, claims \(0.75L_2\le\widehat L\le3.3L_2\) for every stated initialization before \(T_4=\min\{t\ge0:b_2(t)\ge0.5\sqrt{\lambda_1\eta/2}\}\). Here \(L_2=(\lambda_2/2)(1-ab_2)^2\). To exclude a transcription-scale explanation, use the favorable intended surrogate \(\widehat L_c=(\lambda_2/2)(1-Ab_2)^2\), with \(A=\sqrt{2/(\lambda_1\eta)}\). The lower comparison still fails.
analysis: Set \(\lambda_1=100\), \(\lambda_2=1/100\), \(\eta=1/10\), and \((a,b_1,b_2)=(1/3,3/2000,11/10)\). These values satisfy the stated initialization and pre-stopping conditions. Even using the favorable intended normalization of the surrogate, direct substitution at \(t=0\) gives losses \(0.00129065045\) and \(0.00200555556\), whose ratio is \(0.64353762<0.75\). The lemma's lower bound therefore fails without relying on the omitted scale factor.
result: Lemma 4.5's stated universal lower comparison is false on its claimed domain. This invalidates that quantitative component of the analysis; it does not demonstrate failure of the observed training phenomenon.
repair: For \(r=Ab_2\le1/2\) and \(u=a/A\in[\sqrt{0.55},\sqrt{2.1}]\), the ratio \(((1-r)/(1-ur))^2\) lies between \(0.631504254974859\) and \(3.295443406779994\). Thus replace the lower constant on this pre-threshold domain; the stronger upper bound \(1\) survives when \(a\le A\). The first discrete crossing may overshoot and needs separate treatment.
problems.impact_rationale: The exact admissible counterexample falsifies a quantitative lemma used in the main edge-of-stability analysis, beyond a transcription error. This substantial mathematical failure warrants Major.

problems.title: The symmetric three-feature restriction is not the claimed Euclidean gradient-descent reduction
claim: Paraphrase: Appendix C, PDF pp. 14–15, adds an independent relevant feature \(x_3\) having the same variance as \(x_2\), sets the target to \(x_2+x_3\), and considers symmetric initialization \(b_2=b_3\). After substituting this equality, it identifies the resulting loss with the original model after replacing \(\lambda_2\) by \(2\lambda_2\), and asserts equivalent gradient-descent dynamics.
The equality of restricted loss values is correct. The equivalence of Euclidean gradient updates in the chosen common coordinate is not.
analysis: For a symmetric loss \(F(b_2,b_3)\), the tied loss \(g(b)=F(b,b)\) has derivative \(g'(b)=\partial_2F+\partial_3F=2\partial_2F\). The original symmetric Euclidean update uses \(b^+=b-\eta\partial_2F\), whereas unadjusted gradient descent on \(g\) uses twice that change. Equal restricted loss values therefore do not imply the claimed equal-learning-rate dynamics.
result: The asserted Euclidean-GD equivalence for the higher-dimensional extension fails; equality of restricted loss values and preservation of symmetry remain valid.
repair: The tied-coordinate embedding induces metric \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1,2)\). Use the reduced update \(\theta^+=\theta-\eta\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1/2)\nabla F\), or an orthonormal sum coordinate with target amplitude \(\sqrt2\), before transferring the theorem.
problems.impact_rationale: The claimed extension has a factor-two error in its relevant-coordinate update; the original two-feature dynamics and theorems are not refuted by this extension error.

problems.title: Decreasing bounds on gradient-flow-solution sharpness do not imply stepwise monotonicity
problems.source_location: Introduction, PDF p. 2; Section 5.1 and Theorem 5.2, PDF pp. 8–9.
claim: The discussion on PDF p. 2 and Section 5.1, PDF pp. 8–9, presents the result as a decrease of gradient-flow-solution (GFS) sharpness along gradient descent. The precise Theorem 5.2 encloses this sharpness between functions that decrease as \(b_2\) increases. The text also uses a near-monotonic description. This analysis does not assert that Theorem 5.2’s displayed enclosing bounds are false. It checks whether the stronger interpretation, monotonicity of the exact GFS sharpness at every GD step, follows. It does not.
analysis: The gradient-flow invariant is \(\gamma=a^2-b_1^2-b_2^2\). With the model's unit target normalization, zero loss has \(b_1=0\) and \(ab_2=1\), so \(q=a_\infty^2=(\gamma+\sqrt{\gamma^2+4})/2\) determines the limiting state used for GFS sharpness. Decreasing upper and lower envelopes do not imply a decrease of the exact quantity at every discrete gradient-descent step. The near-monotone description and displayed envelopes can remain valid despite a small local increase.

For \(\lambda_1=100\), \(\lambda_2=0.01\), \(\eta=0.1\), and admissible \(\theta_0=(1/3,1/1500,1)\), two projected-GD updates leave projection inactive. The exact invariant difference is \[\gamma_2-\gamma_1=\frac{4884795542280911349753184700897}{12611344042968750000000000000000000000}>0.\] Since \(q\) increases with \(\gamma\) and the \(\lambda_1q\) branch dominates, exact GFS sharpness increases from approximately \(64.98729109\) to \(64.98730259\). This is compatible with decreasing envelopes and near-monotone wording.
result: The stronger stepwise-monotonic interpretation is not implied by the theorem. Its displayed decreasing envelopes and the paper's near-monotone qualification are not refuted.
repair: Describe decreasing envelopes or a near-monotone trend rather than strict all-step monotonicity of exact GFS sharpness.
problems.impact_rationale: The exact local increase only limits a stronger monotonic reading; the stated envelopes and near-monotone qualification remain viable.
